title: Footprint-robust temporal atlas of NYC Citi Bike use, 2023–2024
description: Normalized seasonal and hour-of-week profiles will be similar in the full system and a balanced cohort of stations observed throughout 2023–2024. Members will have stronger weekday morning and evening peaks, while casual riders will have broader weekend-afternoon use. Conversely, the 2024/2023 increase in trips will be materially smaller within the balanced station cohort than systemwide, suggesting that raw growth partly reflects trips at newly or intermittently observed locations. These are unverified, preregistered expectations rather than established findings.
research_questions: Raw Citi Bike trends can conflate changes in use at existing locations with growth of the station network. NYC reported continued expansion during this period, including reaching its 2,000th station in 2023 (https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2023/11/mayor-adams-dot-commissioner-rodriguez-lyft-expansion-improvements-citi-bike-system). Prior research already documents seasonality, weekday commute peaks, and member–casual differences (DOI: 10.1016/j.tra.2016.08.030; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768325/). The useful question is therefore whether these patterns—and especially year-over-year growth—survive a fixed-footprint comparison. The analysis will remain descriptive: trip histories cannot establish station availability, neighborhood exposure, or the causal effect of expansion.
proposed_methods:
In the campaign container, enumerate the Citi Bike archive, download the 2023–2024 monthly files, and audit one schema. If data cannot be obtained or read, stop and report this without generating results. Process files monthly. Parse local timestamps; separately count records removed for missing/unparseable timestamps, end times at or before starts, and durations over 24 hours; repeat key summaries with a 12-hour ceiling. Retain trips lacking station IDs in systemwide totals but not cohort analyses; exclude unknown rider classes only from rider-type comparisons. Inspect daylight-saving hours.

Define the balanced cohort as start-station IDs with at least one valid trip in every month of both years, a trip-data proxy rather than proof of continuous operation. Test a relaxed threshold of 10 months per year and, if straightforward, reconcile ID changes by name and coordinates. Note that the panel favors active, persistent stations and is not neighborhood-representative.

Produce: (1) monthly trips per calendar day for the full system and cohort, split by rider type, with annual totals, 2024/2023 ratios, peak/trough months, and peak-to-trough ratios; (2) normalized 7×24 start-time heatmaps by rider type, year, and footprint; and (3) predefined weekday morning (07:00–09:59), evening (16:00–18:59), weekend afternoon (12:00–17:59), and commute-peak indices. Compare profiles using percentage-point differences, Jensen–Shannon distance, and peak classifications. Decompose trip-count change into cohort and other-station trips as descriptive accounting, not causal attribution. Compute calendar-week block-bootstrap intervals from daily/hourly aggregates; use cross-year consistency as the main replication check. Save code, aggregate tables, figures, and a 3–5-finding report. Documentation: https://citibikenyc.com/system-data.
expected_outcomes: A transparent baseline showing monthly peak and trough, weekday/weekend hourly structure, and member–casual contrasts, with every finding backed by a figure or table.
A direct estimate of how much apparent year-over-year growth attenuates when the observed start-station footprint is held fixed.
A robustness assessment distinguishing stable temporal profile shapes from volume changes caused by the evolving set of observed stations.
A reproducible, memory-efficient workflow with explicit exclusion counts, uncertainty intervals, sensitivity analyses, and no causal claims.
hypothesis: Normalized seasonal and hour-of-week profiles will be similar in the full system and a balanced cohort of stations observed throughout 2023–2024. Members will have stronger weekday morning and evening peaks, while casual riders will have broader weekend-afternoon use. Conversely, the 2024/2023 increase in trips will be materially smaller within the balanced station cohort than systemwide, suggesting that raw growth partly reflects trips at newly or intermittently observed locations. These are unverified, preregistered expectations rather than established findings.
alternatives_considered: A weather-elasticity analysis was rejected because weather effects and member–casual differences are well studied, while purpose would be inferred only indirectly. An e-bike versus classic-bike analysis was considered but lacks fleet-availability, charging, and pricing denominators, making behavioral interpretation weak. Holiday or Friday-transition analysis is feasible but narrower than the campaign questions. The fixed-footprint design adds a concrete sensitivity analysis while still delivering all required descriptive results.
falsification_check: The central footprint hypothesis is weakened if the full-system and balanced-cohort 2024/2023 growth rates differ by less than five percentage points, a reporting threshold rather than a literature-derived cutoff. Shape robustness fails if the peak or trough shifts by more than one month, predefined peak classifications change, or normalized profiles show substantively large percentage-point differences. The rider-type hypothesis fails if members do not have a higher commute-peak index than casual riders in both years, or if member–casual contrasts reverse across years. Large changes under the relaxed cohort, coordinate reconciliation, or 12-hour duration ceiling would indicate that the result depends on data-quality or cohort choices and must be reported as unstable.
unresolved_disagreements: A station’s appearance in every month is only a proxy for availability and induces survivorship toward busy stations; no trip-only definition fully resolves this.
Station-ID changes may make the balanced cohort too small unless name/coordinate reconciliation is reliable.
The five-percentage-point attenuation criterion is pragmatic and should not be presented as a universal threshold.
Without station capacity or service-area population denominators, the study cannot distinguish expansion, increased capacity, and increased demand at existing locations causally.

decision.rationale: Idea B answers every required campaign question (monthly seasonality, day-of-week/hour profiles, member vs casual differences) while adding a genuinely new and decision-relevant angle: whether the headline patterns survive holding the station footprint fixed. That is new knowledge rather than re-verification — it separates 'more trips happened' from 'already-served areas were used more intensively', and the confound it targets is documented (NYC DOT reported ~194 new stations in fiscal 2024 and the 2,000th station in Sept 2023), so the concern is evidence-based, not speculative. It is the most feasible option: trip files alone, no weather merge, no regression packages, month-by-month aggregation that fits the container's constraints, and an explicit stop-if-no-data plan. Its design is the strongest against misleading results: normalized heatmaps so system size cannot mechanically drive shape, pre-stated refutation criteria, sensitivity definitions of the stable cohort, separate accounting of excluded records, DST handling, and honest limits (it cannot prove stations were operational, and the decomposition is descriptive, not causal). It directly serves the campaign's 'good result' definition: 3–5 findings each backed by a figure, with cleaning and limitations stated.
not_chosen: Idea A: The e-bike vs classic angle is interesting, but the design cannot support its behavioral interpretation: e-bike usage is supply-constrained (fleet size, charging, and the January 2024 member pricing change), so differences in seasonal or hourly patterns cannot be attributed to rider preference without availability/denominator data — a confound Idea B explicitly identified when rejecting this same angle. It also uses only 2024, giving no cross-year robustness check, offers no uncertainty quantification, and its core hypothesis (flatter winter curve due to lower exertion) is speculative. The novelty is thinner than claimed, since e-bike vs classic comparisons already exist.

Idea C: The template-transfer test is well constructed, but its central contrast — member demand more predictable than casual demand — is already documented in prior work (e.g., the DC study reporting R² of 0.816 vs 0.427), so H1 partly re-verifies a known result. The residual-weather analysis (H3) partially revives the weather-elasticity framing the group already rejected for lack of novelty, just relabeled as prediction gain. The forecasting framing also drifts from the campaign's descriptive short-report goal, and it carries more moving parts (WMAPE, baselines, label audit, optional weather) without a correspondingly clearer answer to the required questions. Its label-audit component is valuable but does not by itself carry the study.

## p02 pre-meeting presentation

### 1. My understanding of the question and the real gap

The campaign’s required descriptive questions are straightforward: establish monthly seasonality, weekday/weekend hourly profiles, and member–casual differences in 2023–2024. However, simply reporting “winter trough, warm-season peak; weekday commute peaks for members; weekend afternoon activity for casual riders” would mostly reproduce well-established findings.

The more useful gap is:

> **Are those temporal conclusions robust to Citi Bike’s changing geographic footprint, or are apparent changes partly caused by adding stations and neighborhoods?**

This matters because Citi Bike was actively expanding during the proposed study period. NYC DOT reported 194 new stations during part of fiscal 2024 and explicitly attributed some ridership growth to expansion and added capacity. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/operations/downloads/pdf/pmmr2024/dot.pdf?utm_source=openai)) Earlier, the system had reached its 2,000th station in September 2023. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2023/11/mayor-adams-dot-commissioner-rodriguez-lyft-expansion-improvements-citi-bike-system?utm_source=openai))

**My proposed framing:** estimate every major temporal pattern twice—once for the whole system and once for a fixed cohort of stations present throughout both years. The central hypothesis is that **the shapes of the seasonal and hour-of-week profiles will be robust, while the apparent growth in volume will be substantially smaller in the fixed-footprint analysis** *(my claim, unverified)*.

There are no campaign experimental results or `idea_id` findings yet to cite.

---

### 2. What prior work has established

- NYC Citi Bike work already shows that trip generation varies by season, weekday versus weekend, and subscriber/casual status; proximity to transit and land use also matter. DOI: **10.1016/j.tra.2016.08.030**. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965856416307716?utm_source=openai))
- A study using roughly 43 million Citi Bike rides found a **bimodal weekday profile consistent with commuting** and a **single broad weekend peak**, with greater use in warmer months. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768325/?utm_source=openai))
- The “explorer versus commuter” distinction and differences across peak periods, weekdays/weekends, and user types have also been documented. DOI: **10.1371/journal.pone.0232957**. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0232957&type=printable&utm_source=openai))
- Recent work specifically compares members and casual riders, including pandemic-related changes, so member–casual contrasts alone are not a major open question. DOI: **10.1016/j.tbs.2024.100793**. ([trid.trb.org](https://trid.trb.org/View/2362175?utm_source=openai))
- Station-level temporal heterogeneity is also established: Citi Bike stations can be clustered into distinct weekday and weekend demand profiles. DOI: **10.1016/j.tre.2023.103361**. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tre.2023.103361?utm_source=openai))
- The official trip-history archive includes ride timestamps, stations, and member/casual classification, which are sufficient for the proposed analysis. ([citibikenyc.com](https://citibikenyc.com/system-data?utm_source=openai))

**Synthesis:** prior work establishes the expected patterns, while official evidence shows that the system footprint was changing. I did not find the basic descriptive question commonly presented as a **full-system versus fixed-station-cohort sensitivity analysis**. That assessment of the literature is *(my claim, unverified)*, rather than evidence that nobody has ever done it.

---

### 3. Main research idea

## Footprint-robust temporal atlas of Citi Bike usage, 2023–2024

### Question

How much do conclusions about seasonality, commute peaks, member–casual differences, and year-over-year growth change when the analysis holds the station footprint fixed?

### Hypothesis

1. The full system will show a pronounced winter trough and late-summer or autumn peak.
2. Members will show stronger weekday morning and evening peaks; casual riders will have a broader afternoon profile, especially on weekends.
3. These **normalized temporal shapes** will replicate in a stable-station cohort.
4. The 2024-versus-2023 increase in trip volume will be materially attenuated after restricting to that cohort, indicating that some raw growth reflects network expansion rather than greater use of already-served locations.

All four are *(my claims, unverified)*.

### Data and cleaning

Use all 2023 and 2024 monthly trip files available or downloadable from the official archive **from within the campaign container**. First enumerate the archive rather than guessing filenames. If the files cannot be obtained or read in the container, stop and report that as required.

For each row:

- Parse start and end timestamps.
- Remove and separately count:
  - missing or unparseable timestamps;
  - end time at or before start time;
  - duration greater than 24 hours, with a sensitivity analysis at 12 hours.
- Retain records lacking station ID for systemwide temporal totals, but exclude them from fixed-station analysis and report that exclusion separately.
- Exclude unknown rider categories only from member–casual comparisons.
- Treat timestamps as NYC local clock time and explicitly inspect the daylight-saving transition hours.

### Fixed-footprint definition

Primary stable cohort:

- Start-station IDs with at least one valid originating trip in **every month of both 2023 and 2024**.

Sensitivity definitions:

- Stations observed in at least 10 months of each year.
- If computationally easy, check whether results change when stations are matched by rounded coordinates and name, since station IDs may occasionally change *(potential data-quality concern; my claim, unverified)*.

This analysis cannot measure true station availability or days with zero rides from trip records alone. Therefore, “stable” means continuously observed in the trip data, not proven continuously operational.

### Concrete comparisons and outputs

**Figure 1: Monthly volume and fixed-footprint sensitivity**

- Valid trips per calendar day by month.
- Lines for:
  - all stations;
  - stable stations;
  - member and casual riders.
- Table of annual totals, 2024/2023 ratios, peak month, trough month, and peak/trough ratio.
- Decompose the 2024–2023 trip difference into trips originating at stable versus non-stable stations. This is descriptive accounting, not a causal expansion estimate.

**Figure 2: Day-of-week × hour heatmaps**

Produce 7×24 start-time heatmaps for:

- members, 2023 and 2024;
- casual riders, 2023 and 2024;
- full system and stable cohort.

Normalize each heatmap to percentages within rider-year, so system size does not mechanically determine its shape.

**Figure 3: Simple temporal indices**

Predefine:

- **Weekday morning share:** 07:00–09:59.
- **Weekday evening share:** 16:00–18:59.
- **Weekend afternoon share:** 12:00–17:59.
- **Commute-peak index:** weekday morning plus evening share divided by weekday 11:00–15:59 share.

Report these by month, rider type, and year. Use calendar-week block bootstrap intervals, or, if package constraints make that cumbersome, show variation across months and treat replication across the two years as the principal robustness check.

### What would refute the hypothesis?

The proposed interpretation would be refuted or substantially weakened if:

- fixed-cohort and full-system year-over-year growth differ negligibly—for example, by less than about five percentage points;
- peak or trough months move by more than one month under the fixed-cohort restriction;
- full-system and stable-cohort hour-of-week profiles yield different peak classifications;
- members do not have a higher commute-peak index than casual riders in either year; or
- the member/casual profiles fail to replicate directionally across 2023 and 2024.

The five-percentage-point criterion is a proposed reporting threshold, not a literature-derived natural cutoff.

### Why it matters

This distinguishes two statements that are often conflated:

- “More Citi Bike trips occurred,” and
- “People in already-served areas used Citi Bike more intensively.”

It also tests whether familiar commute/leisure interpretations generalize across an expanding service area. The result would remain descriptive and non-causal, but it would produce a more defensible short report than raw totals alone *(my claim, unverified)*.

### Feasibility

This is feasible with trip files alone and needs no weather merge, regression package, or external geographic covariates. Processing can be done month by month, retaining only aggregate tables and station-month counts, so tens of millions of rows need not be held in memory simultaneously.

The briefing notes that the container currently lacks the data and common analysis packages, and that one guessed 2023 filename returned 404. The first implementation step should therefore be a lightweight archive-listing/download script and a one-file schema audit. If access fails, the analysis must stop rather than simulate or invent results.

---

### 4. Alternatives considered

1. **E-bike versus classic-bike temporal substitution.**  
   This is operationally interesting because e-bike use grew rapidly, and annual membership benefits changed in January 2024. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2023/11/mayor-adams-dot-commissioner-rodriguez-lyft-expansion-improvements-citi-bike-system?utm_source=openai)) I do not prefer it because bike availability, charging, fleet composition, and pricing would make behavioral interpretations difficult without denominator data.

2. **Holiday and “Friday transition” analysis.**  
   This could test whether Friday resembles weekdays or weekends and quantify holiday anomalies. Similar transitional-day patterns have already been reported in cross-city work, and the topic is narrower than the campaign’s main questions. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19294?utm_source=openai))

**Recommendation:** use the fixed-footprint robustness analysis as the main contribution, while still delivering the requested basic seasonal, hourly, and member–casual findings.

# p01 pre-meeting presentation

## 1. Where the real gap is
The assigned task is descriptive: seasonality, hour-by-day-of-week profiles, and member vs casual riders. Weather is optional. Last round's proposal was rejected on novelty because weather elasticity by rider type is well studied. I think the gap is not in finding another pattern. It is in saying how much of the variation a calendar explains, where that explanation breaks down, and whether the member/casual label means the same thing in both years.

## 2. What prior work establishes
- **Weather and Citi Bike.** A study on 12 months of Citi Bike data (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0966692318307282) found that time of day matters most, then precipitation. A related multi-city summary reports usage rising with temperature up to about 27–28 °C and then declining. Weekday usage is bimodal or trimodal, and weekend usage peaks around 2–3 pm. (I couldn't tell from the snippet whether the multi-city findings belong to that paper or a companion one.)
- **Member vs casual.** A recent DC paper (https://findingspress.org/article/161506-spatial-dependency-patterns-in-weather-enhanced-bike-share-demand-forecasting-in-washington-dc) found member demand more predictable (R² = 0.816) than casual demand (R² = 0.427). It also found casual demand correlates more strongly with temperature (r = 0.70 vs 0.29, from the Citi Bike December 2023 analysis it builds on). These are one month, one place and a spatial grid, so they don't give a full-year hour-of-week picture.
- **Predictability.** A public repo (https://github.com/mrrishit909/citibike-demand) already forecasts daily Citi Bike trips for 2023–2025 with calendar plus weather models. It also flags that a month's file holds trips that *end* in that month. So the descriptive deliverable is well-trodden, and the audit details matter.
- **Data access.** Per the same repo, 2023 comes inside a yearly file. A blog (https://medium.com/@calvinluozhengpei/from-wall-street-to-central-park-decoding-nycs-citi-bike-patterns-part-1-3155569278cf) lists 2024 names as `YYYYMM-citibike-tripdata.csv.zip` for Jan–Apr and `.zip` for May onward. That blog is about 16 months old, so the names need checking against the S3 index. This fits the screening note that a guessed 2023 filename gave a 404.

## 3. Main idea: a calendar-template transfer test, with a residual audit
**Question.** How much of Citi Bike's hourly and daily variation is fixed by the calendar? Where does a 2023 calendar template fail in 2024, and is the failure explained by weather, a growth shift, or changes in what the data records?

**Hypotheses (pre-stated).**
- H1: A 2023 template of month × day-type × hour, scaled by one 2024/2023 growth factor per rider type, predicts 2024 hourly counts better for members than for casual riders. Error is measured as weighted median absolute percentage error (WMAPE) on held-out hours.
- H2: The largest template failures cluster in specific cells. Casual riders in warm-season weekend afternoons should fail most, and members in the 8 am and 5 pm weekday peaks least. Failures should also cluster in the cold-season shoulder months and on holidays.
- H3: Adding hourly temperature and precipitation to the 2024 residuals (rather than refitting everything) removes a larger share of the casual error than the member error. This is a prediction-gain claim only, not causal.

**Method.**
- **Data.** Download the 2023 and 2024 trip files. Assign each trip to its local `started_at` date and hour, not the file month. Drop duplicate `ride_id` values, rows with missing timestamps, durations ≤ 0 or very short, and durations over about 24 h. Report each count removed. Aggregate to counts by hour × rider type × bike type (classic/electric).
- **Descriptive deliverables (Q1–Q3).** Monthly totals with the peak and trough and their ratio. Weekday and weekend hourly profiles by rider type, with a commute-peak share. Uncertainty comes from variation across weeks (block bootstrap over weeks), since individual trips aren't independent.
- **Transfer test.** Fit the template on 2023 and predict 2024. Compare it against a seasonal-naive baseline of same hour-of-week and month, unscaled. Compare error by rider type, hour-of-week cell and month. Test whether the 2024 error is explained by weather using one weather source (Open-Meteo or NOAA Central Park), and say so as a limitation.
- **Label audit.** Compare duration and bike-type mixes of casual and member trips in the same cell across 2023 and 2024. If casual riders in weekday commute hours look like members (short trips, similar profile), "casual" is a mixed label. That is a concrete use of the "definition changed" limitation.

**What would refute it.**
- H1 fails if the member and casual WMAPE confidence intervals overlap, or if the ranking flips.
- H2 fails if errors are spread uniformly across cells.
- H3 fails if the weather gain is equal for both rider types.
- Whichever way these go, the report shows the template's accuracy, not just a pattern.

**Why it matters.** It gives a quantified version of "members are predictable commuters, casual riders are weather-driven leisure". It also shows which parts of that story fail out of sample, and it makes the report's findings testable instead of merely illustrative. Operationally, it shows which hours can be planned from a calendar and which need live weather.

**Feasibility.** The data is public, and the container has outbound internet (from the screening note). Packages would need pip-installing, ideally DuckDB for aggregation, which avoids loading about 36M rows per year into memory. Weather is optional and can be dropped without losing the core. The design is much lighter than the rejected proposal: no spline GLM or week fixed effects, just template fit, prediction error and bootstrap.

## 4. Alternatives I considered
- **Rejected proposal (weather elasticity by hour-of-week × rider type).** Already judged not novel, and the "purpose vs label" inference is indirect. My version keeps the cell structure but tests prediction rather than fitting elasticities.
- **Clustering stations or trips by temporal profile.** Interesting, but it moves toward spatial analysis, which the task doesn't ask for. It also needs the station table and more tuning.

I prefer the main idea because it covers every required question, adds a pre-stated test, and stays doable if weather data turns out to be hard.

**Questions for the group:**
1. Should we use only 2023 → 2024, or add a placebo (a 2022 → 2023 template) to see whether the 2023 → 2024 error is unusual?
2. How should we treat holidays and the major storm days in the cell-level error?

I agree with the reviewer’s feedback from the screening: simply describing weather effects and member-vs-casual differences is too well-trodden to be novel. To elevate this while still strictly answering the campaign's four questions, we need a fresh lens. 

Here is my presentation for the meeting:

**1. Understanding of the question and the real gap**
The campaign asks for standard descriptive usage patterns (seasonality, commute peaks, member vs. casual). The gap is that treating all bikes as a monolith ignores the massive operational shift to e-bikes. E-bikes cost more to deploy and charge, but we don't know if they merely scale up overall demand or if they fundamentally change *when* the system is used. 

**2. Prior work**
- **Temporal patterns:** It is well established that Citi Bike functions as commuter infrastructure with a pronounced 5 PM peak, and that members commute while casuals ride for leisure (e.g., various 2024 spatial analyses on Medium).
- **Data quirks:** The S3 data format changed over time, but 2024 data includes the `rideable_type` field and is available as monthly zip files. Importantly, the system automatically caps rentals at 1,500 minutes for classic bikes and 480 minutes for e-bikes (Spatial Workflow, Oct 2026); these artificial spikes in the long tail must be cleaned.
- **The gap:** While it is known e-bikes are faster and popular for longer trips, a direct comparison of the *temporal and seasonal elasticity* of e-bikes vs. classic bikes is less common.

**3. ONE main research idea**
- **Question:** Do e-bikes reshape the temporal and seasonal demand of bike-share, or do they just scale it up uniformly?
- **Hypothesis:** E-bikes have a flatter seasonal curve (less drop-off in winter because they require less physical exertion in the cold) and a sharper commute-to-midday ratio on weekdays compared to classic bikes, especially for members.
- **Method:** 
  - Download the 2024 Citi Bike monthly zip files from S3 (the correct URL format is `https://s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata/YYYYMM-citibike-tripdata.zip`).
  - Clean the data: drop negative durations and the capped rentals mentioned above.
  - Compute monthly volume by `rideable_type` to calculate the winter-to-summer volume ratio.
  - Compute hourly volume by `rideable_type` and `member_casual` on weekdays vs. weekends to calculate the peak-to-midday volume ratio.
  - (Optional) Correlate daily volume with temperature separately for e-bikes and classic bikes.
- **What would refute it:** If the seasonal amplitude and commute peak ratios are identical between bike types, the hypothesis is refuted (meaning e-bikes just uniformly add volume without changing behavioral patterns).
- **Why it matters:** It perfectly answers the campaign's four questions but adds a crucial operational dimension. As operators shift to e-bikes, they need to know if this changes *when* bikes need rebalancing and battery-swapping.
- **Feasibility:** Highly feasible. Since the container has internet but no pre-installed data or pandas, we can write a script to download the zips and pip-install `duckdb`. DuckDB can query the raw CSVs efficiently without blowing up RAM, outputting just the aggregated stats we need for plotting.

**4. Alternatives considered**
- *Alternative 1:* A spatial analysis of inter-borough trips (e.g., do e-bikes cross bridges more often?). I prefer the main idea because spatial analysis requires geofencing or spatial joins which are harder without extra shapefiles, and it doesn't directly answer the campaign's mandatory temporal questions.
- *Alternative 2:* A pure replication of the previous weather elasticity proposal with better models. I prefer the main idea because the reviewer explicitly rejected the weather/member angle for lack of novelty. The e-bike angle provides the necessary fresh perspective.

score.explanation: Novelty (4): Seasonality, weekday commute peaks and member/casual differences are well documented (the proposal cites this itself), so the descriptive atlas is incremental. The one more original element is the fixed-footprint (balanced station cohort) comparison, which separates network expansion from usage growth at existing stations. That is a sensible but fairly standard panel-style control, and the expected result (raw growth overstates same-station growth) is close to a foregone conclusion. Feasibility (8): The data are public monthly trip files. The container reached S3 (a guessed filename gave a 404, so the host responds, but the real archive filenames still need enumerating, which the plan already includes). The container has 128 CPUs and 112 GB of free disk. Python 3.11 is installed but pandas is not, so a pip install is needed, or duckdb/polars could be used. The data volume (about 70M trips over two years) is manageable with monthly chunked processing. The methods are clear and bounded: explicit exclusion counts, a relaxed-threshold sensitivity check, block bootstrap on aggregates, and a stop condition if the data cannot be read. Remaining risks are the ID changes and schema drift, the cohort definition (a station active in all 24 months can be a small and biased subset), and an incomplete or 404-prone archive layout. Significance (4): The result would be useful as a methodological caution about interpreting raw Citi Bike growth, and it would give a clean reproducible baseline. It is purely descriptive, with explicitly no causal claims, and the cohort is not representative of the neighborhoods. It would therefore have limited effect on practice or on new research directions. Overall: a competent, honest and executable descriptive study with modest novelty and impact.
